short_definition: Application Programming Interface, a set of defined rules and protocols that allows different software applications to communicate and share data with one another.
simple_explanation: An API is a digital messenger or bridge. Instead of building every feature from scratch, an app uses an API to ask another service for information—such as a rideshare app using Google Maps API to show directions or an online store using PayPal's API to process payments.
job_context: APIs appear in almost every developer job description. Frontend engineers consume APIs to display live data, backend engineers build and secure APIs, and QA testers write automated tests to verify API endpoints.
example: A food delivery app uses the Twilio SMS API to automatically text customers a notification when their order has been picked up by the delivery driver.
source: W3C Architecture of the World Wide Web & IEEE API Design Standards

short_definition: Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment, an automated methodology that continuously builds, tests, and delivers code changes into production.
simple_explanation: CI/CD is like an automated assembly line and safety inspection for code. Every time a developer saves new code, automated servers immediately run tests to make sure nothing is broken, package the application, and deploy it to users without manual intervention.
job_context: CI/CD is a cornerstone practice in modern software teams. Job descriptions for DevOps engineers, software developers, and cloud engineers routinely ask for experience with CI/CD tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins.
example: When a developer merges their bug fix into the main branch on GitHub, the CI/CD pipeline automatically runs 200 automated tests and deploys the updated code to live servers within 5 minutes.
source: IEEE Software Engineering Best Practices for Continuous Delivery

short_definition: The technical process of releasing, installing, and configuring tested software from a development environment onto live servers where end users can access it.
simple_explanation: Deployment is the moment a software project 'goes live' to the world. It is like opening the doors on grand opening day: your code moves from your private workshop onto public servers so that anyone with a web browser or phone can start using the new features.
job_context: The meaning of deployment shifts slightly depending on the role: software developers see it as delivering a tested feature branch, while cloud and DevOps engineers manage the live traffic routing, server scaling, and zero-downtime rollouts.
example: After a team finishes testing an upgraded search algorithm, they execute a deployment at midnight so customers wake up to the faster search experience the next morning.
source: ACM/IEEE Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK v3.0)

short_definition: A pre-built foundation and collection of standardized code libraries that provides a structured template for developing software applications.
simple_explanation: A framework is like a pre-fabricated house frame. Instead of manufacturing every single wooden beam, nail, and electrical socket yourself, the framework gives you the sturdy structure and plumbing, allowing you to focus on decorating and designing the specific rooms.
job_context: Job postings rarely ask for just a language; they ask for specific frameworks. For example, Python postings frequently ask for Django or FastAPI, JavaScript postings ask for React or Angular, and Java postings ask for Spring Boot.
example: Instead of writing thousands of lines of code to handle web requests and database connections manually, a developer uses the Django framework to launch a secure web app in one afternoon.
source: IEEE Standard Glossary of Software Engineering Terminology

short_definition: A centralized digital storage location where all source code files, assets, documentation, and the complete revision history of a project are managed.
simple_explanation: A repository (commonly nicknamed a 'repo') is the dedicated digital folder for a software project. It stores all your project files alongside a detailed history log of every single change ever made, who made it, and why.
job_context: On day one of an engineering job, your manager will grant you access to the company's code repository on GitHub or GitLab so you can clone the codebase to your laptop and start reviewing the code.
example: A junior developer clones their team's mobile app repository to their laptop so they can run the app locally and begin fixing an open issue.

short_definition: Software whose original source code is made freely available to the public for anyone to inspect, modify, enhance, and redistribute.
simple_explanation: Open source is like a community recipe where the master chef shares all ingredients and steps online. Anyone around the world can cook it, suggest new seasonings, fix mistakes, and share improved versions freely with everyone else.
job_context: Companies rely heavily on open-source technologies (like Linux, Python, and PostgreSQL). Contributing to open-source projects is one of the best ways for beginners to gain real-world experience and catch the attention of tech recruiters.
example: A college student fixes a typo and adds a unit test to an open-source data library on GitHub; the maintainer accepts the contribution, making it visible to recruiters.
source: Open Source Initiative (OSI) - The Open Source Definition

short_definition: The on-demand delivery of computing resources—including storage, processing power, servers, and software—over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.
simple_explanation: Cloud computing is like using electricity from a power grid. You do not need to build your own power generator in your backyard; you simply plug into the wall and pay only for the electricity you actually use. Cloud computing gives businesses the same flexible access to computer servers.
job_context: Most modern businesses have migrated their systems to the cloud, making cloud computing knowledge a critical requirement for developers, data engineers, and systems administrators.
example: A video streaming platform uses cloud computing to automatically spin up 100 extra virtual servers during a popular live sports broadcast and shuts them down when the game ends.
source: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Definition of Cloud Computing (SP 800-145)

short_definition: A software system that tracks, records, and manages incremental changes made to source code files and documents over time.
simple_explanation: Version control ensures that you never have messy filenames like 'Project_Final_v2_really_final.zip'. Instead, the system automatically tracks every modification, lets multiple engineers edit the same files simultaneously without conflicts, and allows you to roll back any mistake.
job_context: Version control (primarily using Git) is a non-negotiable prerequisite for nearly all technical job postings across software development, data engineering, and technical writing.
example: When a software update introduces an unexpected bug that slows down checkout, the engineering lead uses version control to safely revert the code back to the stable build from yesterday.
source: ACM/IEEE Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK v3.0)

short_definition: An organized, structured electronic collection of data stored and accessed computationally from a computer system.
simple_explanation: A database is like a supercharged, highly organized electronic filing cabinet. Unlike a basic spreadsheet that slows down with too many rows, a database can safely store millions of customer records, search through them in milliseconds, and ensure multiple people can write data at the exact same moment without corrupting files.
job_context: Database knowledge (especially relational databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL using SQL) is a core requirement for backend developers, data analysts, data scientists, and systems administrators.
example: When you sign into a social media app, the application queries a database to retrieve your profile picture, friend list, and recent notifications in a fraction of a second.
source: C.J. Date - An Introduction to Database Systems & ACM SIGMOD Standards

short_definition: A systematic, phased process used by engineering teams to design, develop, test, deploy, and maintain high-quality software applications.
simple_explanation: The SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is the recipe book for building reliable software. Instead of jumping straight into coding and hoping for the best, teams follow clear stages: planning what to build, designing how it works, writing the code, thoroughly testing it, deploying it to users, and maintaining it over time.
job_context: Understanding the SDLC is fundamental for entry-level developers so they understand how their daily coding tasks fit into the broader company timeline, testing stages, and release schedules.
example: During the testing phase of the SDLC, QA engineers run automated test suites to find and report bugs before the software is released to paying customers.
source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 - Systems and Software Engineering: Software Life Cycle Processes

short_definition: An iterative approach to project management and software development that emphasizes delivering small, working increments of software with rapid feedback.
simple_explanation: Rather than spending two years planning and building a massive software system in secret only to discover users dislike it, Agile teams build small, functional pieces in short cycles (usually 2 weeks). They show their progress to users, gather feedback, and continuously adjust their direction.
job_context: Agile is the dominant working methodology in the software industry. Job descriptions frequently state: 'Experience working in an Agile/Scrum cross-functional team environment.'
example: An engineering team uses Agile principles to release a basic version of a new search filter within two weeks, gathering user feedback before spending time building advanced filtering options.
source: The Agile Manifesto (agilemanifesto.org) & Project Management Institute (PMI) Agile Practice Guide

short_definition: A popular, structured Agile framework where cross-functional teams deliver working software in fixed-length iterations called sprints.
simple_explanation: Scrum provides specific rules and routines for Agile teams. Teams work in 1-to-4-week 'sprints', hold a brief 15-minute daily meeting called a 'standup' to share what they accomplished and what is blocking them, and review their progress at the end of each sprint.
job_context: New hires will immediately participate in Scrum rituals: daily standup meetings, sprint planning sessions, and retrospectives where the team discusses how to work better together.
example: During the 15-minute morning Scrum standup, a junior developer tells the team: 'Yesterday I finished the login screen styling, today I will connect it to the authentication API, and I have no blockers.'
source: The Scrum Guide (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland - scrumguides.org)
